System-1 Orchestration for Enterprise Conversational Agents: Typed Decisions Beside the LLM on τ²-Bench Airline

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-11-22
Status: Submitted to Preprints.org on 22 November 2026 (manuscript ID 245718, under screening); the DOI will be added here when assigned.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/jev-tau2-harness
Keywords: conversational agents; tool calling; τ²-Bench; decision models; LLM orchestration; latency; guardrails

Abstract

Tool-calling chat agents spend most of a customer’s wait on serial LLM calls, and many of those
calls make decisions that a small typed-decision model or plain code can make exactly. We present a
decision-model harness, which places a decision model, one that answers yes/no and multiple-choice
questions, beside the agent’s LLM rather than in front of it. For our experiments we use Jev, a
hosted decision model that answers in about half a second. One Jev call per turn decides whether the
turn needs a tool, which of the customer’s reservations it is about, whether flight statuses matter,
whether the customer confirmed a write, and the route and date of a flight search, while a
speculative model call runs; code then issues those tool calls in one batch and checks every write
against the airline policy. On τ2-Bench Airline (50 tasks × 4 trials, Gemini 2.5 Flash as the
simulated customer) we compare three agent models alone and inside the harness. Code issued 77–84%
of all tool calls and model calls per turn fell by 24–37%. pass4, the share of tasks solved on all
four tries, rose on all three models, by 10.7 points on average, and nearly doubled on the weakest
model, Gemma 4 26B A4B (0.220 to 0.420). Conversations with a policy-forbidden write fell from 43 to
10. pass1 rose on Gemma (0.465 to 0.560) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.810 to 0.860) and fell slightly on
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. Cost fell 17% and 25% on the two Gemini models. Reply latency fell at every
percentile on Flash-Lite (median −31%, p90 −44%); on Gemini 3.8 Flash, tool-using turns were 43%
faster but the slowest turns were not. On four further open models of 30–35B parameters (50 tasks ×
1 trial), the harness raised pass1 by 6–12 points on the three that started below 0.70 and made
tool-using turns 22–41% faster on all four.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Tool calls issued by code: 0% → 76.7–84.4% (all three models)
- Model calls per customer turn: 3.01 → 1.91 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 2.50 → 1.90 (Flash-Lite); 2.17 → 1.58 (Gemma)
- pass4: 0.740 → 0.800 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 0.540 → 0.600 (Flash-Lite); 0.220 → 0.420 (Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- pass1: 0.810 → 0.860 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 0.760 → 0.735 (Flash-Lite); 0.465 → 0.560 (Gemma)
- Conversations with a policy-forbidden write: 43 → 10 (5 → 0, 9 → 3, 29 → 7)
- Agent cost per conversation: $0.0388 → $0.0323 (−17%); $0.0151 → $0.0113 (−25%); $0.0062 → $0.0065
- Reply time to first token, Flash-Lite: median 4.18 → 2.87 s (−31%); p90 12.51 → 7.05 s (−44%)
- Four further open 30–35B models (50 × 1): pass1 +6 to +12 points on the three below 0.70; tool-using turns 22–41% faster on all four
  (All numbers from Tables 3–5 and the abstract of the paper. Gemini 3.8 Flash latency comes from a separate side-by-side 50 × 1 run.)

Choosing Affordable Language Models for Serial Fiction: Instruction Following, Creative Writing, and Story Memory

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-09-26
Status: Published on Zenodo on 26 September 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22977925.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/webnovel-harness
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22977925
Keywords: LLM creative writing; serial fiction; instruction following; story bible; long-context memory; model selection; affordable language models; AI-assisted writing

Abstract

Our goal is to identify an affordable set of language models and prompting practices that can help a
broad community of authors begin and sustain AI-assisted serial fiction. We compare six models
priced below one US dollar per million input and output tokens through 687 chapter-generation
attempts, covering instruction detail, output constraints, reasoning settings, story bibles,
retrieval, history compression and sequential continuation. A selected novel provides a common
reference. We distinguish following the author’s brief from resembling the reference and from
writing an engaging scene. In a 144-attempt instruction-design comparison, 108 drafts were usable,
but only 44 also met the length requirement. Reference-event coverage increased from 4.7% with vague
direction to 90.7% with detailed prose instructions; numbering the same instructions yielded 88.9%
and no consistent advantage across scenes. DeepSeek V3.2 led the selected detailed-instruction
checks, GLM 5.3 Flash was the most balanced creative-scene candidate in exploratory AI readings, and
Tencent Hy3 was the most reliable writer in that comparison. Story-bible updates introduced
different risks, including retained contradictions and unexecuted repairs. The findings support
choosing models by role, specifying causal requirements and creative freedom separately, and
validating both chapters and memory updates. They are practical starting points from a single-novel
study, not a universal literary ranking.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Writing attempts in the study: 687 across five experiment groups
- Instruction-design test: usable drafts / also met length: 108 of 144 usable; 44 met the 1,233–1,667-word band
- Original events supported, by brief: Vague 4.7%; concise 32.7%; detailed prose 90.7%; numbered 88.9%
- Numbering the same instructions (paired, scenes A/B/C): −4.2, −4.8 and +3.7 percentage points: no consistent advantage
- Full-brief requirements supported (detailed + numbered): DS3.2 97.0% (12 of 12 usable); Hy3 93.3% (12 of 12 usable)
- Hy3 with reasoning disabled vs a 1,024-token reasoning hint: Usable 2/8 → 8/8; met length 0/8 → 6/8; median time about 80 → 18 s
- Exact output constraints, all six rules together: 1 of 36 stress-test attempts (a DS4 draft)
- Summary-heavy vs full history (50 prior chapters), cost per usable chapter: −80% Gemini Lite; −56% GLM; −71% DS3.2
  (Numbers from the abstract, Tables 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 15, and Section 3.3. Literary judgments in the paper are exploratory AI readings, not a human reader panel.)
